sections.h2: Where a Colorado eviction case is filed
sections.html:
Evictions go through the state court system. Colorado has 23 judicial districts, and each has a district court and a county court with limited jurisdiction. A residential eviction case lands in the county where the rental house sits, so a landlord who owns houses in two counties may end up with two cases in two courts, each with its own clerk.

The Colorado Judicial Branch runs a Residential Evictions self-help page that sorts its material into guides, step-by-step forms, subpoenas, frequently asked questions and extra resources. The forms for house, apartment and condo evictions are gathered in one place there. A landlord or tenant who cannot afford the filing fee can ask to file without paying, and the Court Resource Centers can point people to help.

Before anything is filed, there is a notice. The type you serve depends on why the tenancy is ending, and it sets the clock for everything that follows. A wrong or late notice usually means starting over, so confirm the form and the deadline with the court or an attorney before you serve it.

Changing the locks, shutting off utilities or carting away belongings is a fast way to end up as the defendant. The Judicial Branch's guidance on unlawful evictions says landlords must follow the right process, and a tenant whose landlord skips it can file a lawsuit.

A tenant who wins can get two kinds of relief:

  • Money from the court, called damages.
  • An injunction from a district court, which stops the unlawful eviction while the case is pending.

An owner who plans to sell a rented house gets no shortcut from the sale. The tenancy continues until it is ended through the court process, and a pending sale contract does not change that.

The forms for an unlawful eviction suit follow a five step order. The deadline for the landlord's answer depends on which court the case is in.

StepWhat happensForms or timing
1Tenant starts the caseComplaint, JDF 601 cover sheet for district court, Form 1 summons for county court or JDF 600 for district court
2Tenant serves the landlordJDF 98 Affidavit of Service
3Landlord respondsDue within 14 days in county court, 21 days in district court
4Hearing preparationJDF 71 witness list, JDF 72 exhibit list, subpoena forms
5As neededJDF 205 motion to waive the filing fee; restraining order motion in district court

The restraining order motion has no standard form, and it belongs to the district court process only.

If you are the landlord and you get served, do not let the answer date slide. A missed deadline in a case like this hands the other side an easy win, and a sale that was already in motion can stall while you sort it out.

sections.h2: Choosing the right notice before you sell
sections.html:
Your choice of notice drives how long you wait and whether the buyer gets a vacant house. Match it to the real reason you are ending the tenancy, and serve it the way the court forms describe.

An owner who wants to sell has a few paths:

  • Serve the notice that fits the situation, then sell after the tenant leaves.
  • Sell the house with the tenant still in it, to a buyer who agrees to take it that way.
  • Agree on a move-out date with the tenant in writing.
  • Sell for cash as is and let the buyer handle the occupancy question.

Each path costs something in time. A buyer who needs a vacant house waits for the tenant to leave. A buyer who accepts an occupied house does not.

A written agreement with the tenant is often the cleanest option, because it can set the move-out date, the condition of the house and what happens to the deposit without a court case. Keep a copy, and give the buyer a copy of the lease and any notices that were served.

sections.h2: Taxes when you sell a rental house
sections.html:
A house that was never your residence does not qualify for the home sale exclusion. That exclusion covers up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, and only for a main home that passes both the ownership and use tests, each of which needs 24 months in the five years before the sale.

Colorado follows the federal figure. Income from real property in the state, capital gains included, counts as Colorado source income. A landlord who lives out of state will usually see the closing agent withhold 2 percent of the sale price or the net proceeds, whichever is less, and the landlord claims that amount on a Colorado return.

If you did live in the house at some point, part of the exclusion may still apply. Ask a tax professional before you decide how to price or time the sale.

Expect paperwork even when the gain is small. If you receive a Form 1099-S, the sale goes on your return even if the gain is excludable, and it must be reported whenever you cannot exclude all of it. Schedule D and Form 8949 are the usual places to report it.

Colorado adds its own return. Nonresidents with Colorado source income file a Colorado return when they have to file a federal return or when they owe Colorado tax. Withholding at closing is claimed on the line for form DR 1079, not the W-2 or 1099 line, and a refund comes back if the amount withheld is more than the tax owed.

Keep the closing statement, the lease, repair invoices and any insurance claim paperwork in one folder. If a tenant dispute turns on repairs, dated photos and records of what the tenant reported, and when, carry more weight than memory does.

Whichever route you choose, a short folder of documents saves days later. Gather the signed lease, the record of rent paid and unpaid, copies of every notice you served along with proof of how and when it was delivered, and any filings if a case has already started. If a tenant raised repair complaints, add the dated requests and what was done about each one.

With that folder, a buyer or the title company can see the real status of the tenancy at a glance. Without it, questions pile up at closing and the date can slip. If a case is already filed, give the buyer the case number and the hearing date so the contract can be timed around them.

sections.h2: Problems landlords run into when selling
sections.html:
Three things slow most rental sales: a tenant who stops paying, a lease that runs past the date you wanted to close, and a house that needs work. A standard listing suffers from each, because lenders and buyers generally want a vacant, move-in ready home.

A cash sale as is removes several of those obstacles. We buy houses in Colorado in their current condition, including rentals with tenants in them, and we can talk through the notice timeline with you before you commit to anything.

This page is general information and not legal advice, so confirm forms and deadlines with the court or a Colorado attorney.

faqs.q: Can a Colorado tenant sue a landlord for an unlawful eviction?
faqs.a: Yes. If a landlord skips the legal process, the tenant can file a lawsuit and may be awarded damages.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to answer a tenant's unlawful eviction case?
faqs.a: The response is due within 14 days in county court and 21 days in district court.

faqs.q: Where do I find Colorado eviction forms?
faqs.a: The Colorado Judicial Branch gathers the forms for house, apartment and condo evictions on its Residential Evictions self-help page.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with a tenant in it in Colorado?
faqs.a: Yes, but the tenancy continues until it is lawfully ended. A buyer who will take the house occupied, or a cash buyer, is usually the fastest route.

faqs.q: Is the gain on a rental house sale taxable in Colorado?
faqs.a: It can be. A house you never lived in does not meet the federal use test, and Colorado treats gain from Colorado real property as Colorado source income.
